notes.h: Demands of the coach or choreographer
notes.b: A coach (or a choreographer, who creates and teaches a dance or movement routine) is a non-playing role, but it is demanding. The performers depend on this person for knowledge, organisation and safety, so the job asks for much more than turning up to sessions.
points: Technical knowledge of the activity: its skills, tactics and rules or, for a choreographer, the movement and composition of the routine. Without it the coach cannot teach correctly or spot errors.
Knowledge of fitness, psychology and safety, so the coach can plan suitable training, support the performers' confidence and focus, and manage the risk of injury.
Planning and organisation of sessions, equipment and the programme over a season, so that training builds towards the competitions that matter.
Time commitment for sessions, travel, preparation and reviewing performance. Much of the work happens outside the training hour.
Managing a group, including keeping everyone involved, resolving conflict and treating each performer fairly, so the team stays united.
Making selection decisions (who plays or performs), which must be fair and explained, otherwise performers feel resentful and trust in the coach falls.
Duty of care: responsibility for the safety and welfare of performers while they are under the coach's supervision.

Safeguarding in Ireland: people working with children in sport must be Garda vetted (checked by the police) and complete child-safeguarding training under their governing body's procedures, which protects young performers from harm.
notes.tip: If asked to identify three demands, pick distinct ones, for example technical knowledge, planning and duty of care, and say briefly what each involves. Only mention Garda vetting and safeguarding training at this level of detail.

notes.b: Interpersonal skills are the skills used when dealing with other people. A coach can know the activity perfectly and still fail if performers cannot understand, trust or approach them.
points: Clear communication and active listening (giving full attention to what the performer says, not just waiting to speak), so instructions are understood and the performer's concerns are heard.
Empathy: understanding how the performer feels about their performance, so the coach responds to a nervous or disappointed performer in a helpful way.
Patience and approachability, so performers feel able to ask questions rather than staying silent when they are confused.
Enthusiasm that motivates the group, because performers tend to copy the energy of the person leading them.
Fairness and consistency in selection, discipline and feedback, so performers know the same standards apply to everyone.
Tact when delivering criticism, so that it is accepted rather than resented.
Leadership and emotional control under pressure, so the coach stays calm and gives clear direction during a difficult match or rehearsal.
notes.tip: Questions often give a scenario in which a coach's instruction is misunderstood. Name a skill, such as clear communication or active listening, and say how it would have prevented the problem. Describe two skills, not just list them.

notes.h: Personal and technical qualities for successful coaching
notes.b: Beyond interpersonal skills, successful coaches share certain personal qualities (what kind of person they are) and technical qualities (how well they coach the activity). Examiners ask you to discuss both.
points: Personal quality, integrity: being honest with performers and selectors about performance and decisions, which builds trust.
Personal quality, patience: teaching new skills at the performer's pace rather than the coach's, because rushing leads to poor technique.
Personal quality, resilience: recovering from losses and keeping the group focused, so a bad result does not derail the season.
Personal quality, commitment to the performers' development rather than personal recognition, so decisions are made for the performer's benefit.
Technical quality, demonstration: showing skills accurately so that performers can copy them.
Technical quality, analysis: identifying the cause of an error, such as a poor body position behind a missed shot, so the coach corrects the cause rather than the symptom.
Technical quality, practice design: designing practices that match the demands of the activity so that training transfers to competition.
notes.tip: Keep the two groups separate in a discussion answer: give personal qualities and technical qualities, and for each one say why it makes the coaching more successful.

notes.b: A goal gives training a purpose. Coaches break a big ambition into smaller steps, and they guide the performer to set goals rather than simply handing them over.
points: Short-term goals cover days to weeks and act as steps towards the long-term goal, so the performer sees regular progress.
Long-term goals cover a season or more and describe the bigger target the performer is working towards.
Agree goals together, using the performer's performance analysis as the starting point, so the goals fit the real strengths and weaknesses and the performer is committed to them.
Write the goals down so that both coach and performer can refer to them and are not relying on memory.
Review goals regularly and adjust them when circumstances change, for example after an injury or a big improvement.

notes.b: A vague goal such as "get better" is hard to act on or check. SMART is a checklist that turns a goal into one a performer can work towards and measure.
points: SMART stands for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time-bound.
Specific: the goal states exactly what is to be achieved, so there is no doubt about the target.
Measurable: the goal has a number or observable outcome that shows progress, so the performer knows when it has been met.
Achievable: the goal is reachable with effort at the performer's current level, so it challenges without being impossible.
Realistic: the goal fits the time, resources and ability available, such as the number of training sessions per week.
Time-bound: the goal has a deadline or review date, which keeps the performer working towards it.
SMARTER adds Evaluate and Review, so the goal is checked and revised rather than set and forgotten.
notes.tip: The syllabus form is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Time-bound. Say what each letter means for a named goal rather than only writing out the words.

notes.b: Goals can focus on three different things. Coaches use all three, but they favour the ones the performer can actually control.
points: Outcome goal: the result, such as winning a match.
Performance goal: a personal standard, such as getting 80% of first serves in.
Process goal: a technique focus, such as a high ball toss on the serve.
Performance and process goals are more within the performer's control than outcome goals, which also depend on the opponent. A performer can hit every target and still lose to a stronger opponent.
notes.tip: Give a tennis-style example for each type if asked to distinguish them, and say that performance and process goals are more controllable than outcome goals.

notes.h: Designing a fitness and skills programme
notes.b: A programme for a specific performer is built in a logical order: start with where the performer is, then plan how to get to the goal. The coach applies methods and principles taught elsewhere, such as FITT (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type), to one real person.
points: 1. Analyse the performer through fitness tests and skill analysis, so the programme starts from their real strengths and weaknesses.
2. Set goals from the analysis, then choose fitness methods and skill practices that match them.
3. Apply FITT and the principles of training and effective practice. There is more on this in Designing a fitness plan and Skill acquisition.
4. Plan weekly sessions with progression (gradually increasing the demand), starting from where the performer is.
5. Monitor the performer and adjust the programme when results or fatigue show a need, because a plan that never changes will not fit a performer who is improving or tiring.

notes.b: How the coach communicates decides whether performers understand and act on the coaching. Good communication is clear, checked and positive.
points: Short, clear instructions with a few key teaching points, not long explanations, because performers can only take in and remember a small amount at once.
Demonstrations show the performer what the skill or sequence should look like, which is easier to copy than a verbal description.
Questioning checks understanding, for example by asking the performer to explain the key point back.
Positive body language, with eye contact and an open stance, shows the coach is interested and approachable.
Feedback that is specific, timely and constructive, such as praise, then correction, then praise, so the performer hears what to fix without losing confidence.
Language adjusted to the performer's age and level, so a beginner or a child is not confused by technical terms.
notes.tip: Describe how a coach gives feedback (specific, timely, constructive), not the definitions of feedback types. Those belong with psychological preparation.

notes.b: A plan rarely survives contact with real performers unchanged. A good coach adapts what is happening as the need arises, rather than carrying on regardless.
points: Simplify or make the task harder to suit the performer's current level, so it stays challenging but achievable.
Change the drill, or add or remove opposition, to make a practice easier or more game-like.
Adapt for injury, fatigue or weather, so that performers stay safe and the session is still useful.
Change tactics or choreography at half-time, based on what the review showed.
A choreographer changes the sequence, formation or timing of the music when a routine does not fit the performers or the space.

notes.b: Performers train harder and for longer when they want to. Coaches use strategies to keep that motivation going through the weeks when progress is slow.
points: Goal setting gives the performer direction and a reason to train.
Variety in sessions keeps training interesting, so performers do not become bored.
Recording progress lets the performer see improvement, which encourages them to continue.
Praise and recognition for effort as well as results, so performers keep trying even when they lose.
Ownership and choice: the performer chooses some drills or goals, which makes them more committed to the plan.
Punishment, such as running laps as a penalty, is avoided as a training tool because it links training with negative feeling. A positive training environment works better.
notes.tip: Give strategies and say how each one keeps the performer motivated. Avoiding punishment as a training tool is a good point to include.

notes.b: Reflection means looking back on a session or performance to learn from it. A coach does not just tell the performer what to think but guides them to reflect for themselves.
points: Training diaries: the performer records what they did, how it felt and what to improve, which builds a record they can look back on.
Video review together, pausing at key moments to discuss them, so the performer sees what actually happened.
Questioning: what went well, and what would you change? This makes the performer do the thinking.
Reflection is linked to the goals of the next session, so what is learned leads to action.

notes.b: Practice time is limited, so time wasted standing around or setting up is time not spent improving. Managing it well means performers get the most useful activity from every session.
points: Session plan with a timing for each activity, so the coach knows what must happen and when.
Equipment set up in advance, so no time is lost during the session.
Minimal waiting: small groups or rotating stations keep every performer active.
Clear transitions between activities, signalled in advance, so the group moves on quickly.
Keep to the plan while allowing flexibility when the session needs changing.
If time runs short, protect the session's main objective first, so the most important work is not the part that gets dropped.
notes.tip: When asked why a coach must manage time effectively, link each point to more activity time or a better session outcome, not just to being organised.

notes.h: Evaluating your coaching against an admired coach
notes.b: The syllabus asks you to analyse your own coaching, using a coach or choreographer you admire as a point of reference. The coach you choose is your own choice.
points: Choose criteria such as communication, planning, motivation, technical knowledge and results, so the comparison is fair and specific.
Compare your coaching with the admired coach's on each criterion, honestly, including where you fall short.
Identify one strength to keep and one area to develop.
Set a specific action to improve the chosen area, such as reviewing video of your own sessions.

keyTerms.definition: The responsibility a coach or choreographer has for the safety and welfare of the performers in their care.
Measures that protect children and vulnerable people from harm, including vetting and child-safeguarding training.
Understanding how a performer feels about their performance and responding to it.
Goals that are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time-bound.
A goal set for days to weeks that acts as a step towards a long-term goal.
A goal set for a season or more.
A goal based on the result of a contest, such as winning a match.
A goal based on a personal standard, such as a level of accuracy or a personal best.
A goal focused on a technique or action that the performer controls, such as a high ball toss.
Information given to a performer about their performance, such as praise or correction.
A written record in which a performer notes what they did, how it felt and what to improve.
A deliberate change to practice or performance in response to a need, such as injury, fatigue or a plan that is not working.

questions.prompt: Discuss the personal and technical qualities needed for successful sports coaching.
questions.model: Personal qualities: integrity, so the coach is honest with performers and selectors; for example, explaining a selection decision truthfully rather than hiding behind vague reasons. Patience, so the coach can teach new skills at the performer's pace; for example, repeating a drill calmly instead of criticising a slow learner. Resilience, so the coach can recover from losses and keep the group focused; for example, planning the next session immediately after a defeat. Organisation also supports these qualities, because sessions and records are planned in advance. Technical qualities: the ability to demonstrate skills accurately so performers can copy them, for example a clear model of a tennis serve. The ability to analyse performance and identify the cause of an error, for example recognising that a poor body position causes a missed shot. The skill to design practices that match the demands of the activity, so that training transfers to competition. Each quality matters because the performer's development depends on the coach's trustworthiness, planning and ability to teach.

questions.prompt: Describe two desirable interpersonal skills of a coach or choreographer and explain how each supports the performer.
questions.model: Active listening: the coach listens to the performer's explanation of how a drill felt before correcting it, so the coaching responds to the real problem and the performer feels heard. Empathy: the coach recognises when a performer is anxious after a poor result and adjusts the next session's demands and tone, so the performer keeps their confidence and motivation.

questions.prompt: Explain why a coach needs to manage practice time effectively and give two ways of doing so.
questions.model: Time lost to waiting or slow transitions reduces the work performers do and the skill they gain, so a coach must manage practice time to make every minute count. First, write a session plan with a timing for each activity and set up equipment before the session, so no time is lost. Second, keep performers active through small groups or rotating stations, so there is minimal waiting.
